flags: A1.5 (results paper, section 1, observed drought and climate effects since 2011): the 22.3% is a simulation of the 2001 to 2020 climate applied to farms with 2015-16 to 2018-19 structure, prices and technology, not a measured fall in profits, and its window starts 2001, not 2011; cite 22.6% (Table 5) or 'about 23%' and say 'simulated'. The 2050 range should name both pathways (-2 to -32% RCP4.5; -11 to -50% RCP8.5). A1.5 pairs L135 Grundy (climate effect on yields under 10% to 2050) with this paper's national wheat yield fall of 2.8 to 24.1% under RCP4.5 (p. 16); the two should be set side by side, not merged.

file_ok: yes: Hochman, Gobbett and Horan 2017, Climate trends account for stalled wheat yields in Australia since 1990, Global Change Biology 23: 2071-2081
what_taken: APSIM simulation at 50 representative sites with observed weather and 2015 management: water-limited wheat yield potential fell 27% (1.23 t/ha; 47 kg/ha a year) from 1990 to 2015 (pp. 2071, 2075); 83% of the fall from lower rainfall, 17% from higher temperatures, with rising CO2 offsetting a further 4% (p. 2077); national actual yields stayed flat as relative yield rose from 39% to 55% (p. 2076).

flags: A1.5 and B8.1: the 27% is a fall in simulated water-limited yield potential, not in actual yields, which did not fall (p. 2076, p. 2079); any line reading 'wheat yields fell 27%' should say 'yield potential'. The series ends in 2015, so for A1.5 ('since 2011') it is context on the climate trend, not a measure of the post-2011 period.
notes: Period 1972 to 1990 showed no significant Yw trend (p. 2075). Authors note APSIM misses frost and heat extremes, so the decline is likely understated (pp. 2077-2078). Implied absolute loss in actual yield about 23 kg/ha a year, offset by technology (p. 2079). why: priority 1 at A1.5; 2 at B8.1; open access no; PDF uploaded by Murray.

flags: A12.1 and B8.2: none that changes a claim. The 11 to 28% is a range across crops, each crop taken alone, not an uncertainty range and not total diet; animal products and feed are left out (p. 233). The paper gives no Australian or Oceania figure in the main text (Oceania only in Supplementary Fig. 4d, p. 230), so it supports the general point that closed local self-sufficiency is rarely possible, not an Australian number.
notes: Local production consumed first in each cell; flows minimise distance or travel time; production from LPJmL scaled to FAOSTAT 2006 to 2010 (pp. 234-235). Halving yield gaps and losses shortens distances mainly in Africa and Asia; little change in Oceania (pp. 230-231). Combining six crops yields one global foodshed (p. 232). why: priority 1; open access yes; PDF uploaded by Murray.
